_note: 1851 cities for the Canadian Rails map. lat/lon are real modern coordinates for the historical site; name is the name IN USE IN 1851. full/shared are the two printed income values. hub = non-developable port (black square). special = one of the three $10 connection cities. region is for terrain authoring and the research doc only.

cities.name: Montréal
cities.note: Commercial capital of British North America; head of ocean navigation. Lachine Canal 1825; St Lawrence dredging began 1850. Trimmed a point (was 7) to help fund raising the lower-St-Lawrence and Huron-shore towns — the trunk corridor was carrying the board's income almost alone.

cities.name: Québec
cities.note: Great timber port and capital of Canada East; the largest shipbuilding centre in BNA. Trimmed a point (was 6) to help fund raising the lower-St-Lawrence and Huron-shore towns — the trunk corridor was carrying the board's income almost alone.

cities.name: Toronto
cities.note: Capital of Canada West; exploded from under 2,000 in 1825. Trimmed a point (was 5) to help fund raising Owen Sound — the southern Ontario core was pulling every company's track toward itself already.

cities.name: Halifax
cities.note: Ice-free Atlantic port and Royal Navy North America station. The Intercolonial's whole objective. Printed at 7/5 rather than its ~20,700 population would suggest: it is 1,240 km from Montréal over the New Brunswick Highlands, and the terminus has to pay for the journey or no company will ever build east.

cities.name: Saint John
cities.note: Largest city in New Brunswick; timber and shipbuilding. With Portland parish adjoining, ~30,000.

cities.name: Hamilton
cities.note: Head of Lake Ontario navigation; the Great Western Railway's home and headquarters.
cities.nudgeWhy: shifted so no two cities touch

cities.name: Kingston
cities.note: Fortress town at the foot of Lake Ontario, on the Frontenac Axis. Former capital.

cities.name: Bytown
cities.note: Renamed Ottawa in 1855 — Bytown in 1851. Rideau Canal terminus and capital of the Ottawa Valley square-timber trade.

cities.name: London
cities.note: Centre of the western peninsula; Great Western Railway on the way.
cities.nudgeWhy: shifted so no two cities touch

cities.name: Trois-Rivières
cities.note: Midway between Montréal and Québec; the St Maurice forges, the oldest industry in Canada.
cities.nudgeWhy: shifted so no two cities touch

cities.name: St. Catharines
cities.note: On the Welland Canal — the lock system that bypassed Niagara Falls.
cities.nudgeWhy: east of Hamilton, on the Niagara peninsula; shifted so no two cities touch

cities.name: Fredericton
cities.note: Capital of New Brunswick, at the head of Saint John River navigation.

cities.name: Portland
cities.note: Maine. Montréal's ice-free winter port — the entire purpose of the St Lawrence & Atlantic, which agreed on 4 August 1851 to meet the Atlantic & St Lawrence at Island Pond.

cities.name: Sherbrooke
cities.note: Capital of the Eastern Townships, on the St Lawrence & Atlantic main line.

cities.name: Belleville
cities.note: Bay of Quinte port on the Toronto–Montréal trunk route.
cities.nudgeWhy: shifted so no two cities touch

cities.name: Pictou
cities.note: The Pictou coalfield. The Albion Mines Railway opened 19 September 1839 — Nova Scotia's first railway and the first genuinely effective steam operation in Canada.
cities.nudgeWhy: shifted so no two cities touch

cities.name: Yarmouth
cities.note: One of the great sailing-ship registries of the age; enormous tonnage for its size.

cities.name: Charlottetown
cities.note: Capital of Prince Edward Island, then a separate colony.

cities.name: Buffalo
cities.note: New York. Erie Canal terminus; the Great Western was built to bridge Buffalo to Detroit across Canadian soil.

cities.name: Detroit
cities.note: Michigan. The western end of that same Great Western land bridge.

cities.name: Chatham
cities.note: Canada West, on the Thames. (Distinct from Chatham, New Brunswick — see the name-collision note in the research doc.)
cities.nudgeWhy: east of Windsor on the Thames; shifted so no two cities touch

cities.name: Windsor
cities.note: Facing Detroit across the river; named Windsor in 1836. (Distinct from Windsor, Nova Scotia.)
cities.nudgeWhy: east of Detroit across the river; shifted so no two cities touch

cities.name: Sorel
cities.note: At the mouth of the Richelieu. Called William Henry 1787–1845, Sorel again by 1851.
cities.nudgeWhy: downstream and west of Trois-Rivières, at the Richelieu mouth; shifted so no two cities touch

cities.name: Saint-Hyacinthe
cities.note: Richelieu valley town on the St Lawrence & Atlantic.
cities.nudgeWhy: south-east of Montréal, on the Richelieu; shifted so no two cities touch

cities.name: Newcastle
cities.note: On the Miramichi — the great New Brunswick timber river. Named for the town, not the later amalgamated Miramichi.

cities.name: The Bend
cities.note: The Bend of Petitcodiac — renamed Moncton only in 1855. Junction of every proposed Intercolonial route; the Saint John–Shediac line opened through here in 1860.
cities.nudgeWhy: shifted so no two cities touch

cities.name: Amherst
cities.note: On the Chignecto Isthmus — the 24 km neck that is the only land route into Nova Scotia.

cities.name: Sydney
cities.note: Cape Breton. The Sydney coalfield, worked by the General Mining Association. Remote but valuable — hence the unusual 2/2.

cities.name: Barrie
cities.note: On Kempenfelt Bay, on the Ontario, Simcoe & Huron (Northern) Railway then under construction toward Georgian Bay.
cities.nudgeWhy: inland on Lake Simcoe, north of the lakeshore chain; shifted so no two cities touch

cities.name: Sault Ste. Marie
cities.note: The rapids between Lakes Superior and Huron; a fur-trade and portage post at the far edge of settlement. Nudged up slightly — even with Owen Sound now a reliable waypoint, measured play showed nobody continued the extra 5 hexes out here.

cities.name: Bruce Mines
cities.note: Canada's first copper mine, opened by the Montreal Mining Company in 1847 and worked by Cornish miners; about 250 people by 1848. Nudged up slightly — even with Owen Sound now a reliable waypoint, measured play showed nobody continued the extra 3 hexes out here.
cities.nudgeWhy: shifted so no two cities touch

cities.name: Chicoutimi
cities.note: Saguenay lumber settlement, founded 1842 — the northern frontier of settlement in Canada East. Value reflects remoteness: a long spur has to pay for itself.

cities.name: Rimouski
cities.note: Lower St Lawrence; last substantial settlement before the Matapédia wilderness. Bumped a notch above pure population: with Fraserville now anchoring the corridor upriver, this stretch needed to read as a route worth building, not just a remote dead end.
cities.nudgeWhy: south bank of the estuary; latitude alone cannot say which bank

cities.name: Fraserville
cities.note: 1851 name for Rivière-du-Loup (renamed back in the 20th century); the Fraser seigneurial family's village, incorporated 1850. Real population outgrew Chicoutimi, Rimouski and Gaspé combined by 1851 — the Grand Trunk later chose it as a terminus (1859). Added to give the lower St Lawrence corridor a genuine mid-route payoff instead of five remote 2/1 stops in a row.
cities.nudgeWhy: shifted so no two cities touch (Rimouski and Chicoutimi)

cities.name: Gaspé
cities.note: Fishing station at the tip of the peninsula, effectively cut off by land. Value reflects remoteness: a long spur has to pay for itself.

cities.name: Campbellton
cities.note: At the Matapédia gap on Chaleur Bay — the single land corridor between Canada East and New Brunswick, and the route Major Robinson recommended in 1849. Value reflects remoteness: a long spur has to pay for itself.

cities.name: Bathurst
cities.note: Chaleur Bay timber port on Robinson's surveyed line. Value reflects remoteness: a long spur has to pay for itself.
cities.nudgeWhy: shifted so no two cities touch

cities.name: St. Andrews
cities.note: Passamaquoddy Bay. The St Andrews & Quebec Railway's locomotive Pioneer landed here in March 1851 — then a strike, a storm and politics stalled the line. Value reflects remoteness: a long spur has to pay for itself.
cities.nudgeWhy: shifted so no two cities touch

cities.name: Pembroke
cities.note: Upper Ottawa Valley square-timber town, settled 1828 — the far end of the pineries. Value reflects remoteness: a long spur has to pay for itself.

cities.name: Owen Sound
cities.note: Georgian Bay harbour, laid out 1840s as the Toronto–Lake Huron portage terminus. Measured play showed it (and Bruce Mines/Sault Ste. Marie beyond it) never got built into even at 2-3 hexes from the core network — a pure value problem, not distance. Raised to match its real population (comparable to Pembroke's) plus a bit more, since this is the one hex the whole northwest arm hinges on reaching.
